subject: Chemistry
title: Taxol: Cancer Drug From a Tree
description: A micro-lesson that makes Taxol: Cancer Drug From a Tree usable.

hook.text: Taxol, one of the most effective cancer drugs ever, comes from the bark of the Pacific yew tree—a slow-growing endangered species.

buildup.text: In 1962, the National Cancer Institute collected bark from a yew tree in Washington State. The extract killed cancer cells.

discovery.text: Taxol stabilizes microtubules inside cells, freezing the machinery needed for cell division. Cancer cells can't split and die.

twist.text: Making one dose required killing six 100-year-old trees. Environmentalists and cancer patients were in direct conflict.

climax.text: Chemists learned to semi-synthesize Taxol from yew needles—no tree killing needed. It now treats breast, ovarian, and lung cancer.

punchline.text: A tree bark that freezes cell division. Nature's chemistry, humanity's cure.

quiz.question: How does Taxol kill cancer cells?
options: It stabilizes microtubules, preventing cells from dividing
It dissolves cancer cell membranes on contact
It blocks blood supply to tumors by collapsing blood vessels

details.summary: Taxol, or paclitaxel, was discovered in Pacific yew tree bark and kills cancer cells by stabilizing microtubules, preventing their normal disassembly during cell division. Cells frozen in mitosis cannot complete division and undergo apoptosis. It required decades to solve massive supply challenges.
details.whyItMatters: Taxol is effective against breast, ovarian, and lung cancers and generates billions in annual revenue. Its supply crisis drove innovations in semi-synthetic production and plant cell culture technology.
takeaways: Taxol stabilizes microtubules, locking cells in mitosis until they die
Pacific yew bark initially provided the only source of this drug
Semi-synthetic methods from renewable yew needles solved the supply crisis

faq.question: Why was the supply of taxol such a controversial challenge?
faq.answer: Producing enough taxol for one patient required bark from six Pacific yew trees, killing them. Environmentalists protested the potential extinction of old-growth yew forests. It took years to develop semi-synthetic production from baccatin III found in renewable yew needles.

faq.question: How does stabilizing microtubules kill cancer cells?
faq.answer: Microtubules must dynamically assemble and disassemble to form the mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes during division. Taxol prevents disassembly, freezing the spindle. The cell cannot complete mitosis and eventually triggers its own death through apoptosis.
